← Sponsor Ready

The GitHub Sponsors readiness checklist: 10 signals, ranked by weight

What Sponsor Ready actually checks, and how much each one is worth. Fix the top of this table first — it is ranked by weight for exactly that reason.

All 10 checks, highest weight first

Weights sum to 100. This is a heuristic against public signals, not a GitHub eligibility rule.
Points Signal One-line fix
30A valid FUNDING.yml is presentAdd .github/FUNDING.yml with at least one funding platform.
12Pushed to within the last 90 daysShip a commit — even a small docs or dependency update.
10README makes a visible sponsorship askAdd a short "Support this project" section near the top of the README.
10README is a real onboarding doc, not a stubCover what the project does, why it exists, and how to start in the first screen.
8Repo has a descriptionSet a description in the repo's "About" panel.
8At least 3 topics setAdd topics in the "About" panel describing what the project does.
8A license file is presentAdd a LICENSE file — GitHub's repo creation UI can generate one.
6CONTRIBUTING guide is presentAdd a CONTRIBUTING.md describing how to file issues and submit changes.
4A homepage / live demo link is setSet the repo's homepage URL to a demo, docs site, or landing page.
4A CODE_OF_CONDUCT is presentAdd a CODE_OF_CONDUCT.md — GitHub's community health template is a reasonable default.

The gap between the top and bottom of this table is deliberate, not arbitrary: FUNDING.yml alone is worth as much as the bottom five items combined. A repo can have a perfect README, a license, topics, and a code of conduct, and still show no Sponsor button to a single visitor, because that button's existence depends on one file none of those other signals touch.

Run the checklist against a real repo — your own, or this tool's own repo as a worked example — to see which of these ten it currently passes and fails.

This is an informational heuristic against publicly documented signals, not a GitHub eligibility rule. It is not affiliated with GitHub and does not guarantee any sponsorship outcome or approval.

Common questions

What does it actually take to look ready for GitHub Sponsors?

There is no official eligibility checklist from GitHub for how a repo looks to a visitor. This page lists the 10 publicly-checkable signals Sponsor Ready scores, ranked by weight: a FUNDING.yml file (30 points) matters most because it is the file that turns on the Sponsor button at all, followed by recent activity, a visible sponsorship ask in the README, and seven smaller signals covering README quality, discoverability, and community health.

Which single fix improves a Sponsors readiness score the most?

Adding .github/FUNDING.yml with at least one funding platform, for example github: [your-username]. It is worth 30 of the 100 points Sponsor Ready checks for — three times the next-highest single item — because without it a repo has no Sponsor button for a visitor to click at all, regardless of how strong every other signal is.

Sponsor Ready

Free checklist for GitHub Sponsors readiness. Paste a public repo, get a ranked list of what's missing — no signup, nothing stored here.

Not sure what to paste? — it scores the project Sponsor Ready lives in, so you can see the checklist before pointing it at your own work.

Checking…

What this is and isn't

  • Every check runs in your browser, calling GitHub's public API directly. This site has no server and stores nothing about the repos you check.
  • This is an informational heuristic against publicly documented signals — it is not affiliated with GitHub and does not guarantee any sponsorship outcome. It never tells you to enable GitHub Sponsors.
  • Only anonymous, aggregate usage counts (for example "a scan happened") may be recorded locally — never which repo you scanned.

Common questions

Does a high score mean GitHub will approve me for Sponsors?

No. This checklist has nothing to do with GitHub's own Sponsors program eligibility review — it scores publicly documented signals (a FUNDING.yml, a substantial README, recent activity, a license, and similar) that tend to correlate with a repo looking sponsor-ready to a human visitor. It never tells you to enable Sponsors and is not affiliated with GitHub. See all 10 signals ranked by weight, with the one-line fix for each. If you already use GitHub's own Community Standards page, here is how the two differ — this reads the same community-profile data and then asks a different question.

Why did my scan fail with a rate-limit error?

Every check calls GitHub's public API directly from your browser, unauthenticated, which GitHub caps at 60 requests per hour per visitor IP. If you or others on the same network have scanned several repos recently, wait a few minutes and try again — there is no server-side proxy here to work around the limit.

Can I check a private repository?

No. The tool only calls GitHub's public, unauthenticated API, so it can only see what an anonymous visitor to your repo page could see. A private repo returns a 404 and the checklist has no way to read it.

Does it store or send the name of the repo I scanned anywhere?

Your repo target is sent only to api.github.com, the same request your own browser would make visiting the repo page. This site has no server and stores nothing about which repos you check; only anonymous, aggregate usage counts like "a scan happened" may be recorded locally, with an opt-out below.

Can I share a link to a scan result?

Yes. After a scan, "Copy link to this result" puts the repo name in the page's own URL fragment (the part after #), which browsers never send to any server — opening the link just re-runs the same public scan in the recipient's own browser. It only works for public repos, so it never reveals anything that a visit to the repo's GitHub page would not already show.

vs-github-community-standards.html.text:
← Sponsor Ready

Sponsor Ready vs. GitHub's Community Standards

The same community-health data, asked a different question. GitHub's page checks whether the recognised files exist. This one asks what is stopping the repository attracting sponsors — and which fix is worth the most.

They are not rivals — one is built on the other

GitHub's Community Standards page, on a repository's Insights tab, is a completeness checklist for a healthy open-source project: description, README, code of conduct, contributing guidelines, license, issue and pull-request templates, security policy. Every item is a tick or a gap, and every item counts the same.

Sponsor Ready calls GitHub's own community profile API — the same endpoint behind that page — and then asks something narrower: what is stopping this repository attracting GitHub Sponsors? It adds the funding-specific signals Community Standards does not look at, weights everything by how much it actually moves sponsorship rather than treating a code of conduct as equal to a missing Sponsor button, and returns a ranked fix this first list rather than a flat set of ticks.

Nothing here replaces the Community Standards page. It is free, built in, and covers ground this tool deliberately does not score.

What each one looks at

SignalCommunity StandardsSponsor ReadyWeight
A valid FUNDING.yml — what puts the Sponsor button on the reponot checkedchecked30
Recent activity — a project that looks abandoned does not attract recurring fundingnot checkedchecked12
README makes a visible sponsorship asknot checkedchecked10
README is a real onboarding doc, not a stubpresence onlychecked10
Repository descriptioncheckedchecked8
Topics set — how the project gets found at allnot checkedchecked8
License filecheckedchecked8
CONTRIBUTING guidecheckedchecked6
Homepage / live demo linknot checkedchecked4
CODE_OF_CONDUCTcheckedchecked4
Issue templates, PR template, security policycheckednot scored—

The five signals Community Standards does not look at are 64 of the 100 points, and the largest single one is the funding file itself. That is the shape of the gap: a repository can pass Community Standards completely and still have nothing anywhere that lets a willing person give it money.

Two practical differences

It ranks rather than lists. A flat checklist tells you six things are missing; it does not tell you that one of them is worth thirty points and another is worth four. The ordered output is the actual product here — the point is to know which single change to make this afternoon.

It runs on repositories you do not own. Community Standards lives inside a repository's own Insights tab. This runs client-side against the public API, so you can point it at a well-funded project you admire and see how it is set up before copying the pattern. Requests are unauthenticated — which is what keeps the tool account-free — and GitHub caps those at 60 an hour per visitor IP. When you hit that ceiling the page says so, rather than reporting the data it could not fetch as a failing check.

Nothing you enter is uploaded and no account is created: the checks run in your own browser, calling api.github.com directly.

Common questions

Should I use Sponsor Ready or GitHub's Community Standards page?

Use both — they answer different questions, and this tool is built on top of the other one rather than against it. GitHub's Community Standards page, under a repository's Insights tab, checks whether the recognised community-health files are present: a description, a README, a code of conduct, contributing guidelines, a license, issue and pull-request templates, and a security policy. It is a completeness checklist for a healthy open-source project. Sponsor Ready calls GitHub's own community profile API — the same data behind that page — and then asks a narrower question: what is stopping this repository attracting GitHub Sponsors? That adds signals Community Standards does not look at, weights them by how much they matter for sponsorship rather than treating every item equally, and returns a ranked fix-this-first list instead of a flat set of ticks.

What does Sponsor Ready check that Community Standards does not?

Five things, and together they are 64 of the 100 points. A valid FUNDING.yml is worth 30 on its own — it is what puts the Sponsor button on the repository, and Community Standards does not look for it at all. Recent activity is worth 12, because a repository that looks abandoned does not attract recurring funding. A visible sponsorship ask in the README is worth 10, since a funding file nobody is pointed at converts poorly. Repository topics are worth 8, because they are how the project gets found in the first place. A homepage or live-demo link is worth 4. The remaining 36 points cover ground that overlaps with Community Standards — a substantial README, a description, a license, a contributing guide, and a code of conduct — but scores them by weight rather than presence alone.

What does Community Standards cover that Sponsor Ready does not score?

Issue templates, a pull-request template, and a security policy. Sponsor Ready reads whether some of these exist, because they come back in the same community profile response, but it does not award points for them: they matter for contributor experience and for triage load, which is a real thing to care about and simply not the question this tool answers. If you want a complete community-health pass, read the Community Standards page too — it is free, built in, and nothing here replaces it.

Can I run this on a repository I do not own?

Yes, and that is one practical difference. GitHub's Community Standards page lives inside a repository's own Insights tab, so it is oriented around a project you are already looking at as its maintainer. Sponsor Ready runs entirely in your browser against the public GitHub API, so you can point it at any public repository — including a project you admire, to see how a well-funded one is actually set up before copying the pattern into your own. The requests are unauthenticated, which is what keeps the tool account-free, and GitHub caps those at 60 an hour per visitor IP; the page says so plainly when you hit that ceiling rather than reporting the missing data as a failing check.

Is this page affiliated with GitHub?

No. This site is not affiliated with, endorsed by, or sponsored by GitHub or Microsoft. GitHub, GitHub Sponsors, and the Community Standards page are named here only to describe what this checklist is and is not, and no claim is made about them beyond their publicly documented behaviour.

Open the Sponsor Ready checklist to score a repository, or read the checklist writeup for what each signal means.

No warranty. This tool is provided free and as-is, without warranty of any kind, express or implied. It is not legal, tax, or financial advice, and it does not replace a qualified professional. You are responsible for reviewing and verifying its output before relying on it, and for meeting any obligation it helps you prepare for. To the maximum extent permitted by law, the authors accept no liability for any loss or damage arising from its use.

A score is not a forecast. These signals correlate with repositories that attract sponsorship; scoring 100 does not mean anyone will sponsor you, and scoring low does not mean nobody will. The weights are this tool's own judgement, not GitHub's, and no dollar outcome is promised or implied.
